newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-CalPERS sets UK, French governance guidelines.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-CalPERS sets UK, French governance guidelines.

text.p: Highly active U.S. pension fund CalPERS on Thursday launched a set of corporate governance principles for Britain and France but said it did not intend to target specific companies -- at least not yet.

The chief lawyer for the California Public Employees' Retirement System (CalPERS), Kayla Gillan, stressed at a news conference that the principles, which address such issues as independent directors, splitting the role of chairman and chief executive and confidential voting for shareholders, were market rather than company specific.

"At this time, CalPERS does not intend to use the principles for any company-specific matter," she said, brushing aside suggestions that CalPERS, the largest public pension fund in the United States with assets of more than $110 billion, might draw up a "hit list" of poor performers.

But she said that the fund, which has $3.7 billion invested in Britain and $1.9 billion in France and has been particularly active over good governance and seeking boardroom changes in the U.S., would reconsider looking at specific company issues in 1998 or 1999.

The principles build on the underlying concepts that CalPERS sees as fundamental to free and fair markets and are intended to complement corporate codes such as Cadbury and Greenbury in Britain and the Vienot report in France.

Richard Regan, head of investment affairs at the Association of British Insurers and current chairman of the International Governance Committee which is due to meet in Paris in July, welcomed the principles. He said CalPERS was trying to support and develop codes in countries where they exist and encourage their adoption in others.

But he said it had to be recognised that company structures and market cultures differed, so that, for example, abolition of cross-shareholdings in France -- one of CalPERS' recommendations -- could not be done overnight.

Gillan said existing codes should be seen as minimum benchmarks and said CalPERS would like to see overseas investors represented on bodies such as Britain's Hampel committee, which reviews standards for corporate governance.

The principles in some areas go beyond current recommended best practice in Britain. For instance, they argue for a larger majority of independent directors, more regular election of all directors -- ideally all of them every year -- and confidentiality when shareholders vote.
On confidentiality, Gillan said: "In the U.S. it is very common for a company to track how votes come in and pressure shareholders to change their vote, which is a very dangerous thing to happen."
Alan MacDougall, joint managing director of British shareholders' group PIRC, said it was very supportive of the initiative in general but said confidential voting might raise practical problems.
But Gillan said the U.S. system of independent assessors worked well in companies which had adopted confidentiality.
In France, CalPERS recommends a one-share, one-vote capital structure, an end to cross shareholding, the regular election of all directors and greater disclosure of executive pay.
Gillan said there should also be greater disclosure of the nomination process for directors, which she described as "something of a mystery in France."

Gillan acknowledged that CalPERS could not simply export its U.S. view of corporate governance, but said that if the UK, for example, did not have standards which were globally competitive, its market would be priced accordingly.

CalPERS aims to have similar principles outlined for Japan and Germany, its other two main areas of overseas investment, by the end of this year. Gillan said this was taking longer for these markets because they are "harder".
"The UK is the birthplace of corporate governance. Japanese and German structures are so much different that it's a much longer learning curve," she said.
